meta.one_idea: A container is an isolated process on a shared kernel; a virtual machine is a whole operating system on a hypervisor. That one difference decides boot time, size, density and isolation, and so which one a workload gets.
outcomes: Say what a container is, and what namespaces, cgroups and a union filesystem each do.
Name Docker's five parts, tell an image from a container, and run, build and remove a container.
Compare containers and VMs on boot time, memory, image size, density, isolation and security.
Choose a container or a VM for a workload using the decision criteria.
Place VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V, VMware, Docker, Podman and containerd, and use registries and tags.

cards.title: What a container is
cards.purpose: A container is a process on the host's kernel with its own isolated view, and no guest operating system.
cards.heading: Process-Level Isolation
cards.lead: A container is a running process that shares the host machine's kernel but gets its own isolated view of files, network and other processes, with no separate guest operating system of its own
show: Namespaces : limit WHAT a process can see
Control groups : limit HOW MUCH it can use
Union filesystem : layers that build the image itself

cards.title: Docker's five parts
cards.purpose: A client sends commands to a daemon, which builds and runs containers from images pulled from a registry.
cards.heading: Five Core Parts
cards.lead: Docker runs as a client-server system: a command-line client talks to a background daemon that builds and runs containers using images pulled from a registry
show: Docker client: CLI issuing commands like docker run
Docker daemon (dockerd): service building and managing containers
Images: read-only templates stored locally or in a registry
Containers: running instances created from images
Registry: remote store such as Docker Hub for images

cards.title: Isolation strength
cards.purpose: A VM is walled off at the hardware with its own kernel; containers share one kernel.
cards.heading: Kernel Versus Hardware

Shared kernel means one kernel vulnerability can reach every container
VM: A guest OS crash usually does not affect sibling VMs

beats.name: Security Trade-offs Between Containers And VMs

cards.title: Blast radius
cards.purpose: A breakout from a container can reach further than a breakout from a VM.
cards.heading: Blast Radius Differs
cards.lead: Stronger isolation does not mean fewer attacks; it changes how far a successful attack can spread once the boundary is crossed
show: VM breakout may exploit a hypervisor vulnerability and can affect isolation between VMs
Container breakout exploits the shared kernel: mitigated by seccomp, SELinux, non-root users
Untrusted or multi-tenant code favours VM-grade isolation
Trusted internal services accept container isolation for speed and density

Self-hosted option: Harbor, run inside an organisation's own network

cards.title: Tagging strategy
cards.purpose: Tags name versions for people; an immutable tag never moves, latest always does.
cards.heading: Naming Image Versions
cards.lead: Image tags provide human-readable names for versions, while digests identify exact image content for reliable redeployment
show: Semantic versioning: major.minor.patch, for example app:2.3.1
latest tag: moves with every push, unsafe for production rollback
Immutable tag: git-commit hash, for example app:a1b2c3d, never overwritten
Environment tags: app:staging, app:prod mark the pipeline stage
cards.visual_guidance: Timeline of three pushes to one repository, each landing a different immutable tag, with the latest pointer jumping between them
must: latest moves; every immutable tag stays where it landed.

Point 2, <q>latest tag: moves with every push, unsafe for production rollback</q>, appears, and the latest pointer jumps to the newest push.
Point 3, <q>Immutable tag: git-commit hash, for example app:a1b2c3d, never overwritten</q>, appears, and each push gets a commit-hash tag that never moves.
